newsitem.title: UK: Russian opposition paints bleak picture of economy.
newsitem.headline: Russian opposition paints bleak picture of economy.

text.p: Two leading Russian opposition politicians on Saturday painted a bleak picture of Russia's economic prospects, in sharp contrast to an upbeat forecast from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
Alexander Lebed, former general and leader of Russian People's Republican Party, told a conference on eastern and central Europe that anyone wanting to invest in Russia must be mad.
"Long term investment is out of the question," he said. "What insane person would invest in a country where legislation changed all the time?"
The conference Lebed addressed was taking place ahead of the EBRD annual conference in London on Monday and Tuesday.
EBRD first vice president Ronald Freeman said Russia would be "the growth story of 1997".
"We believe that Russia will continue to drive strongly towards increases in its economic growth rate and receptivity to the foreign investment necessary to drive it forward," he said.
Grigory Yavlinsky, head of Russia's opposition liberal Yabloko party, also took a bleak view of the economy, saying a sharp contraction in gross domestic product (GDP) was likely this year.
"It will be a difficult year for economic growth. The best scenario forecast for the year is minus 2.0 to 2.5 percent," he said.
President Boris Yeltsin has forecast that the Russian economy will grow by up to two percent this year but independent economists remain sceptical.
Lebed said the government had failed to create an effective mechanism of political power.

"The state authority is an administrative mutant, people are pressed from the top by the authorities and from below by crime and the thoughtless actions of the authorities have turned everyone in Russia into liars, crooks and thieves," he said.
He slated the government for non-payment of wages and pensions in order to curb inflation and said no other government could have got away with this.
Russia needed to create a middle class as well as a "civilised" stock market, which would overcome people's reluctance to invest long-term.
"I am not just for a mixed economy, but for the multi-level economy," Lebed said, adding the utilisation of all Russia's resources would "jump-start" the economy.
Freeman, who is leaving the EBRD shortly, was much more positive, however.
He applauded the recent appointment of Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov as first deputy prime ministers, saying both were "unequivocally reform-minded".
The EBRD, set up in 1991 to assist central and eastern European countries in the transition to market economies, was holding a separate weekend business forum ahead of its annual meeti.
Freeman said the EBRD was forecasting average GDP growth of three percent for the countries in the region for this year.
"While growth in 1996 lagged that of 1995, the outlook for the current year now looks better than for any year since the EBRD began operations," he added.
